cadence: Daily scheduled review; publication follows verified work.
latestSummary: Two older observational studies were newly indexed, adding adult-persistence and autism-related evidence with important limits. A historical registry audit traced changes in study definitions, not treatment effects.

timeline.title: Check when a definition changed.
timeline.type: Primary-study scan and historical registration audit
timeline.summary: Two newly indexed studies add observations, not treatment proof. A device-trial history also shows changing outcome definitions; the dates alone do not explain why they changed.

timeline.title: Different questions need different comparisons.
timeline.summary: A small severe-adult device study assessed tic videos and daily function using different comparisons. We could not calculate a functional treatment advantage from compatible public aggregates; that is not evidence of no benefit.

timeline.title: Match the score and the clock.
timeline.summary: An implanted-device trial's public score definitions and timing do not yet support a compatible aggregate comparison. We did not calculate treatment effects; this is not a finding of no benefit.

timeline.title: A brain signal is still a clue.
timeline.summary: A brain-recording study analyzed five adults. Timing and statistical-unit gaps limit its interpretation; the observed signals do not establish a cause of tics or a treatment benefit.

timeline.title: What paired outcomes can and cannot reveal.
timeline.summary: Constructed worlds shared identical tic change but differed in pain change. Direct paired measures distinguished some worlds; excluding an entire group made two worlds indistinguishable.

timeline.title: Pain has its own footprint.
timeline.summary: A historical pain-selected survey reported interference with sleep, mood and everyday life. Mixed ages and missing item counts prevent an adult-only estimate.

timeline.title: Ask about pain directly.
timeline.summary: A selected adult survey mixed past and present pain. Conflicting help-seeking counts prevent a reliable care-success percentage; reported usefulness does not establish treatment efficacy.

timeline.title: Measure life beyond tics.
timeline.summary: A behavioral-therapy study did not establish added benefit over supportive therapy on its daily-function measures. Positive responder associations answer a different question.

timeline.title: Who came back matters.
timeline.summary: A behavioral-therapy trial's six-month improvement figure describes returning early responders. Missing follow-ups and planned booster sessions limit claims about lasting benefit for everyone.

timeline.title: Timing changes the conclusion.
timeline.summary: A 2022 adult online behavior-therapy trial missed its primary endpoint. Later benefits remain exploratory, with tic severity, impairment and quality of life kept separate.

timeline.title: A tic score is not the whole story.
timeline.summary: A six-report measurement review keeps tic severity, impairment, and quality of life separate. A reconstructed response table showed 14.66% disagreement between two response labels, not an adult quality-of-life result.

timeline.title: Keep severe adult experiences in view.
timeline.summary: The adult burden review examined published measures and follow-up windows. Sparse visits cannot describe every day between them, and high burden need not depend on waxing and waning.

timeline.title: Ask what missing outcomes could change.
timeline.summary: The median-nerve stimulation follow-up analysis tested missing-outcome scenarios. Reported improvement among returnees did not identify the result for everyone originally included.

timeline.title: An available dataset is not always the right dataset.
timeline.summary: Five cohort families were checked for adult, time-linked observations. No resource demonstrated the full combination needed for the proposed days-and-weeks antecedent question.

timeline.title: Define improvement before combining results.
timeline.summary: Four studies used different ways to identify tic absence. Meaningful improvement and observable tics can coexist. No single pooled remission rate was calculated.

timeline.title: A convincing pattern still needs a test.
timeline.summary: A reproducible cycle-detection benchmark compared repeating fits with future forecasts and nonperiodic baselines. Generated data tested a method, not a biological mechanism.

findings.title: Daily life belongs beside tic counts.
findings.summary: An adult qualitative study highlighted better treatments and practical daily-life priorities. A specialist-clinic sample cannot represent everyone.
findings.label: Isaacs and colleagues, 2024
findings.linkState: Primary text readable via web reader; direct request access-limited

findings.title: Persistence deserves its own attention.
findings.summary: A small blinded adult follow-up found observable tics in some people who reported being tic-free. Observation method changes what a study can claim.
findings.label: Pappert and colleagues, 2003
findings.linkState: HTTP 403 in this retrieval; not established broken

findings.title: Shared improvement is not interchangeability.
findings.summary: Published treatment cohorts can show changes in both tic scores and quality of life. That alone does not show that one measure can replace the other.
findings.label: Ivanova and colleagues, 2026
findings.linkState: Primary PDF retrievable through this check

activities.title: A hand at ease
activities.intro: Gently open and rest one hand in your usual supported position, if that feels comfortable.
activities.seated: Use your usual supported seated position. No stretching or stillness is required.
activities.standing: If standing is already comfortable, keep your usual support and let the hand rest naturally.
activities.rest: Imagine the movement, or rest. There is nothing to complete.

activities.title: A familiar little route
activities.intro: Consider a short stroll or wheel along a familiar level route, using your usual supports.
activities.seated: Stay seated and notice something familiar around you instead.
activities.standing: Choose only a route and movement that already feel comfortable for you.
activities.rest: Stay where you are, imagine the route, or skip it.

activities.title: Notice one comfortable thing
activities.intro: Notice one comfortable sound, shape, or texture nearby.
activities.seated: Look or listen from wherever you are comfortably seated.
activities.standing: If you are already comfortable standing, notice something nearby.
activities.rest: No need to pay close attention. Rest or skip freely.

activities.title: Familiar music, or silence
activities.intro: Choose familiar quiet music if you would enjoy it. Silence is an equal choice.
activities.seated: Listen in your usual comfortable position if you choose.
activities.standing: There is no need to move, dance, or keep a rhythm.
activities.rest: Choose silence, rest, or leave this idea for another day.

activities.title: A small mark or a silly sentence
activities.intro: Make a small mark, or say, type, or imagine a silly sentence.
activities.seated: Use a familiar comfortable way to draw, speak, or type.
activities.standing: If you prefer standing, keep your usual support. Imagining works too.
activities.rest: Do nothing, or imagine something amusing. Either is enough.

activities.title: Rest, or leave the page
activities.intro: Rest can be the whole idea. There is no progress to keep up with.
activities.seated: Settle into your usual comfortable seated position if you want.
activities.standing: Change to a usual comfortable position if that suits you.
activities.rest: Close the page or simply carry on with your day.
